name: The Ottoman Empire
title: Social Hierarchy of the Ottoman Empire: From Sultan to Enslaved
period: 1451–1600 (from Mehmed II to the end of the 16th century)

tiers.name: The sultan
tiers.you: Every office, fortune and life in the ruling class is yours to give or take, and in law the empire’s farmland is yours, but you fought your brothers for the throne, and the law let you put them to death.
tiers.kid: The Ottoman sultan ruled from Topkapı Palace in Istanbul and could appoint or dismiss any official.
tiers.rise: Only a son of the dynasty could reign, and the throne went to the prince who prevailed over his brothers, sometimes before his father’s death: Selim I forced his father Bayezid II to abdicate in 1512.
tiers.why: The sultan, the padişah or “lord of kings”, was the source of every office and, in law, the owner of the empire’s farmland.

tiers.name: Viziers, governors and palace officers
tiers.you: You were taken from a Christian family as a boy and trained in the sultan’s palace; now you command armies and own slaves yourself, but in law you are still the sultan’s slave, and your post, your fortune and your life are his to take.
tiers.kid: Many Ottoman viziers and governors had been taken from Christian families as boys and trained in the sultan’s palace.
tiers.rise: Pages left the palace for posts as officers and governors, and a governor could rise to vizier. A word from the sultan could end a career: Bayezid II had the grand vizier Gedik Ahmed Pasha executed in 1482.
tiers.why: At the top of the ruling class stood the grand vizier, the sultan’s deputy, with the other viziers of the imperial council (divan), the governors-general of the provinces (beylerbeyi), eight in 1527 and 32 by 1609, and…

tiers.name: Provincial cavalry
tiers.you: You collect the taxes of a few villages instead of a salary and keep order there, and when the sultan calls you ride to war with your armed retainers; stay away too long and you lose your grant.
tiers.kid: Ottoman cavalrymen called sipahis were paid with the taxes of villages instead of wages.
tiers.rise: Timars went to cavalrymen’s sons who served, and as rewards to Janissaries and other servants of the sultan; a commoner who distinguished himself in war might also win one.
tiers.why: The provincial cavalry, the timariot sipahis, made up the bulk of the classical Ottoman army.

tiers.name: Religious scholars and judges
tiers.you: You trained in Islamic law in a madrasa and now hear your district’s cases, draw up its inheritances and check its officials; you pay no taxes, and if you began as a teacher you may one day judge a great city.
tiers.kid: Ottoman judges called kadis were trained in Islamic law and settled disputes in every district of the empire.
tiers.rise: Any Muslim boy could enter a madrasa, many of them paid for by pious endowments, so the poor could rise by learning; graduates who took a town judgeship at once were paid sooner but rarely rose as high as those who began as teachers.
tiers.why: The ulama, scholars of Islamic law trained in the madrasas, formed the learned branch of the ruling class and, like the rest of it, paid no taxes.

tiers.name: Janissaries and household troops
tiers.you: You were taken from a Christian household as a boy, converted and trained as a cadet; now you live in barracks on the sultan’s pay, may not marry, and answer to no one but your own officers.
tiers.kid: Janissaries were the sultan’s elite foot soldiers, who lived in barracks and marched to the music of their own band.
tiers.rise: A Janissary rose by seniority within his unit; the best were promoted to the household cavalry or given timars, and a few rose far, like Mimar Sinan, levied in 1512, who commanded Janissary units before becoming the sultans’ chief architect.
tiers.why: The sultan’s standing army, the kapıkulu or “slaves of the Porte”, were salaried professionals: the Janissary infantry and six divisions of household cavalry.

tiers.name: Merchants and guild craftsmen
tiers.you: You keep a shop in the bazaar at a trade that your guild regulates and the state watches over, you pay your taxes, and your sons are spared the levy of boys.
tiers.kid: Ottoman craftsmen belonged to guilds that set standards for their trades and helped members in hard times.
tiers.rise: Guild rights passed within families, and guilds went to court against outsiders who took up their trade; a merchant’s wealth brought comfort and influence, but not a place in the ruling class.
tiers.why: The townspeople were reaya, taxpayers, but the sultans needed them.

tiers.name: Peasants and herders
tiers.you: You farm a hereditary plot that belongs in law to the sultan, give a tenth or more of your harvest to the cavalryman who holds your village, and work some days on his own fields.
tiers.kid: Most people in the Ottoman Empire were farmers, who gave part of every harvest as tax.
tiers.rise: The Ottoman saying ran “the son of a reaya is a reaya”, but a Muslim villager could rise by study in a madrasa, by distinction in war or, from the late 16th century, by enlisting as a soldier.
tiers.why: The great majority of the sultan’s subjects were peasants, the reaya (“flock”) of the countryside, and they paid for the empire.

tiers.name: Christian and Jewish subjects
tiers.you: You keep your church and your community’s courts, but you pay the poll tax, may not bear arms, and every few years the officials may come to take one of your village’s sons for the sultan’s service.
tiers.kid: Christians and Jews in the Ottoman Empire could follow their own religion but paid an extra tax.
tiers.rise: Conversion to Islam lightened taxes and opened the ruling class, and the devshirme carried some village boys to the highest offices; Christians and Jews could also prosper in trade, finance and medicine, and Jewish physicians served the sultans.
tiers.why: Christians and Jews were dhimmis (zimmi), protected peoples under Islamic law.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You were taken in war or seized in a raid and sold in a slave market; you serve in a household or row the galleys, and your hope of freedom rests on your owner’s piety or a promise of release after a fixed term.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and made to work without pay; many were later set free.
tiers.rise: Freedom came by manumission, often after a fixed term of service or by the owner’s will, or for a concubine whose child the owner acknowledged; freed slaves often stayed with their former owners, for few other livelihoods were open to them.
tiers.why: Islamic law forbade enslaving Muslims or the empire’s own Christian and Jewish subjects, so the enslaved were outsiders: prisoners of war, people seized by Barbary corsairs, Africans brought across the Sahara and the…
